Introduce means to bring something or someone into a situation where they were not before — for the first time.

The most important idea is firstness. Every use of "introduce" carries the sense of a beginning, a first encounter, or a new arrival. If something has already been there, you wouldn't use "introduce."

1. To present one person to another (people meeting for the first time)

This is the most everyday use. When you introduce two people, you are the one who makes them aware of each other — you say who the other person is so they can start knowing each other.

  • "Let me introduce you to my sister, Priya."
  • "She introduced her boyfriend to her parents last weekend."
  • "He walked into the room and introduced himself to everyone."

Notice: you introduce someone to someone else. The person being introduced is new to the other person's world.

You can also introduce yourself — meaning you tell someone who you are because they don't know yet.

2. To bring something new into use, existence, or a place

When a company, government, or person brings a new product, rule, idea, or system into the world — something that didn't exist in that context before — they are introducing it.

  • "The company introduced a new smartphone last year."
  • "The government introduced a new tax in 2025."
  • "Europeans introduced potatoes to Asia centuries ago." (the potato was new there)
  • "Our school introduced a no-phone policy."

Here, "introduce" means: to bring something into a place or situation where it didn't exist before.

3. To make someone experience something for the first time

When someone gives you your very first experience of something — a subject, a skill, a hobby, a piece of music — they are introducing you to it.

  • "My uncle introduced me to chess when I was six."
  • "That class introduced me to classical music."
  • "Who introduced you to this author?"

The idea: before this moment, you had no connection to that thing. The person made the first connection happen.

4. To begin or open something (a speech, topic, chapter, show)

When a speaker, writer, or host introduces something, they bring it up at the very start — they open the door to it before going deeper.

  • "The professor introduced the topic by giving a brief overview."
  • "She was asked to introduce the guest speaker at the event."
  • "The first chapter introduces the main character."

Here, "introduce" means: to present something at the beginning, so the audience knows what is coming.

Note: an introduction (the noun) is the opening part of a book, speech, or essay — it is literally where you "introduce" the content.

5. To put or insert something into something else (formal/technical)

In formal, scientific, or technical language, "introduce" can mean physically putting or inserting one thing into another.

  • "The doctor introduced a small tube into the vein."
  • "The chemical was introduced into the water supply."
  • "A new gene was introduced into the cells."

This is the same logic: something is being brought into a space where it wasn't before.

6. To formally propose something (in law or official settings)

When a politician formally proposes a new law to be considered, they introduce a bill.

  • "The senator introduced a bill to protect wildlife."

Again — bringing something new into an official process for the first time.
The Thread Running Through All Meanings

No matter which meaning you look at, one idea stays constant:

Something that was outside is now being brought inside — for the first time.

MeaningWhat is being brought in

Whether you're introducing a person to a friend, a product to a market, a topic to an audience, or a tube into a vein — you are always moving something from outside to inside a relationship, a space, or a situation, and it is always happening for the first time.

If it's the second time, you wouldn't say "introduce." You'd say "mentioned again," "showed again," or "reintroduced" (a separate word meaning to bring back something that was once there but had left).

• Introduce someone to someone — present them to each other: "I'll introduce you to my team."
  • Introduce something to/into a place — bring it there for the first time: "introduce new laws into the country."
  • Introduce someone to something — give them their first experience: "He introduced me to jazz."
  • Introduce a topic/subject — begin talking about it: "Let me introduce today's discussion."
  • Introduce yourself — tell someone who you are for the first time: "Please introduce yourself to the class."

• It does not mean to teach something fully. Introducing a topic just opens it up; teaching goes much deeper.
  • It does not mean to repeat or remind. It is always about a first moment.
  • It does not mean simply to mention. Mentioning is casual. Introducing is more deliberate — you are formally bringing something into a new context.
One Final Way to Remember It

Think of a door. To introduce is to open a door and bring something through it — into a new place — for the very first time.

Once the door has been opened and the thing has come through, the introduction is complete. Everything that follows is a continuation, not an introduction.
